# Page: Amber File Formats

# Amber File Formats

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [benchmark/water/dimos_water.py](benchmark/water/dimos_water.py)
- [benchmark/water/generate_water_box_amber.py](benchmark/water/generate_water_box_amber.py)

</details>



## Purpose and Scope

This page documents the Amber file formats used by DIMOS for defining molecular topologies and coordinates. Amber formats are one of the two primary classical force field input methods supported by DIMOS, alongside GROMACS formats (see [GROMACS File Formats](#7.1)). 

The two key Amber file types covered here are:
- **`.prmtop`** - Parameter/topology files containing force field parameters and molecular structure
- **`.inpcrd`/`.rst7`** - Coordinate/restart files containing atomic positions and box dimensions

For information on how these files are used with the `AmberForceField` class, see [Classical Force Fields](#4.1).

---

## Overview

Amber file formats originate from the AMBER (Assisted Model Building with Energy Refinement) molecular dynamics package. DIMOS uses these formats through the ParmEd library, which provides parsing and structure manipulation capabilities.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "Amber File Formats"
        PRMTOP[".prmtop File<br/>(Parameter/Topology)"]
        INPCRD[".inpcrd/.rst7 File<br/>(Coordinates)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "DIMOS Integration"
        PARMED["parmed.amber.Rst7"]
        AMBERFF["dimos.ff.AmberForceField"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Molecular Data"
        TOPOLOGY["Topology:<br/>Atoms, Bonds,<br/>Force Field Parameters"]
        COORDS["Coordinates:<br/>Positions,<br/>Box Dimensions"]
    end
    
    PRMTOP --> AMBERFF
    INPCRD --> PARMED
    
    AMBERFF --> TOPOLOGY
    PARMED --> COORDS
    
    TOPOLOGY --> SIM["MDSimulation"]
    COORDS --> SIM
```

**Sources:** [benchmark/water/dimos_water.py:58-61](), [benchmark/water/generate_water_box_amber.py:16-18]()

---

## .prmtop File Format

### Purpose and Contents

The `.prmtop` file (parameter/topology file) is a binary or ASCII file containing complete force field parameter information and molecular topology. It stores:

| Category | Contents |
|----------|----------|
| **Atom Information** | Atom types, masses, charges, Lennard-Jones parameters |
| **Connectivity** | Bond lists, angle lists, dihedral lists, improper lists |
| **Force Field Parameters** | Bond force constants and equilibrium lengths, angle parameters, torsion parameters |
| **Exclusions** | Nonbonded exclusion lists (1-2, 1-3, 1-4 interactions) |
| **Periodicity** | Box type and dimensions (if periodic) |

### File Structure

The `.prmtop` file uses a flag-based format where each section begins with a `%FLAG` marker followed by the data format specification `%FORMAT`. Common flags include:

```
%FLAG POINTERS
%FLAG ATOM_NAME
%FLAG CHARGE
%FLAG MASS
%FLAG BONDS_INC_HYDROGEN
%FLAG BONDS_WITHOUT_HYDROGEN
%FLAG ANGLES_INC_HYDROGEN
%FLAG ANGLES_WITHOUT_HYDROGEN
%FLAG DIHEDRALS_INC_HYDROGEN
%FLAG DIHEDRALS_WITHOUT_HYDROGEN
%FLAG LENNARD_JONES_ACOEF
%FLAG LENNARD_JONES_BCOEF
```

### Loading .prmtop Files in DIMOS

```mermaid
graph TD
    PRMTOP_FILE[".prmtop File<br/>on Disk"]
    
    AMBERFF_INIT["dimos.ff.AmberForceField<br/>Constructor"]
    
    PARMED_PARSE["ParmEd Parsing<br/>(Internal)"]
    
    FF_PARAMS["Force Field Parameters:<br/>- Bonded terms<br/>- Nonbonded terms<br/>- Exclusions"]
    
    TOPOLOGY_DATA["Topology Structure:<br/>- Atom list<br/>- Bond graph<br/>- Residues"]
    
    PRMTOP_FILE --> AMBERFF_INIT
    AMBERFF_INIT --> PARMED_PARSE
    PARMED_PARSE --> FF_PARAMS
    PARMED_PARSE --> TOPOLOGY_DATA
```

The `AmberForceField` class constructor accepts a `.prmtop` file path:

```python
dimos_system = dimos.ff.AmberForceField(
    'amber100.prmtop',
    cutoff=10,
    switch_distance=7.5,
    nonbonded_type='PME',
    periodic=True,
    dtype=torch.float64
)
```

**Sources:** [benchmark/water/dimos_water.py:61]()

---

## .inpcrd/.rst7 File Format

### Purpose and Contents

The `.inpcrd` (input coordinate) or `.rst7` (restart) file contains atomic coordinates and optionally velocities and box dimensions. Both extensions refer to the same format, with `.rst7` typically used for restart files from simulations.

| Field | Description | Required |
|-------|-------------|----------|
| **Title Line** | Descriptive text | Yes |
| **Atom Count** | Number of atoms | Yes |
| **Coordinates** | X, Y, Z positions in Ångströms | Yes |
| **Velocities** | X, Y, Z velocities (optional) | No |
| **Box Dimensions** | a, b, c, α, β, γ for periodic systems | If periodic |

### File Format Specification

The coordinate file follows a fixed-format structure:

```
Line 1: Title (free format string)
Line 2: NATOM (number of atoms), optionally TIME (simulation time)
Lines 3+: Coordinates (6 values per line in format 12.7)
         X1, Y1, Z1, X2, Y2, Z2, ... (in Ångströms)
Last line (optional): Box dimensions a, b, c, α, β, γ
```

Coordinates are written in Fortran format `(6F12.7)`, meaning 6 floating-point values per line, each occupying 12 characters with 7 decimal places.

### Loading .inpcrd Files in DIMOS

```mermaid
graph TD
    INPCRD_FILE[".inpcrd/.rst7 File"]
    
    PARMED_RST7["parmed.amber.Rst7<br/>Parser"]
    
    EXTRACT_POS["Extract Positions:<br/>rst7.positions"]
    
    CONVERT_UNITS["Convert to Ångströms:<br/>.value_in_unit(angstrom)"]
    
    TORCH_TENSOR["torch.tensor()<br/>Convert to PyTorch"]
    
    MDSIM["MDSimulation<br/>Initialization"]
    
    INPCRD_FILE --> PARMED_RST7
    PARMED_RST7 --> EXTRACT_POS
    EXTRACT_POS --> CONVERT_UNITS
    CONVERT_UNITS --> TORCH_TENSOR
    TORCH_TENSOR --> MDSIM
```

Loading coordinates in DIMOS uses ParmEd's `Rst7` class:

```python
rst7_file = parmed.amber.Rst7('amber100.inpcrd')
positions = torch.tensor(
    rst7_file.positions.value_in_unit(parmed.unit.angstrom)
)
```

**Sources:** [benchmark/water/dimos_water.py:58-59]()

---

## Complete Workflow: Loading Amber Files

### Standard Loading Pattern

The typical pattern for loading Amber files in DIMOS combines topology and coordinate loading:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Rst7 as parmed.amber.Rst7
    participant AmberFF as dimos.ff.AmberForceField
    participant MDSim as dimos.simulation.MDSimulation
    
    User->>Rst7: Load .inpcrd file
    Rst7-->>User: Return positions
    
    User->>AmberFF: Load .prmtop with parameters
    AmberFF-->>User: Return force field system
    
    User->>MDSim: Initialize with system + positions
    MDSim-->>User: Ready for simulation
```

### Code Example

```python
# Load coordinate file
rst7_file = parmed.amber.Rst7('system.inpcrd')
positions = torch.tensor(
    rst7_file.positions.value_in_unit(parmed.unit.angstrom)
)

# Load topology and create force field
dimos_system = dimos.ff.AmberForceField(
    'system.prmtop',
    cutoff=10.0,
    switch_distance=7.5,
    nonbonded_type='PME',
    periodic=True,
    dtype=torch.float64
)

# Create integrator
integrator = dimos.integrators.LangevinDynamics(
    stepsize=2.0,
    temperature=300,
    friction=1.0,
    system=dimos_system,
    dtype=torch.float64
)

# Initialize simulation
simulation = dimos.simulation.MDSimulation(
    dimos_system,
    integrator,
    positions,
    temperature=300
)
```

**Sources:** [benchmark/water/dimos_water.py:58-65]()

---

## ParmEd Integration

### Role of ParmEd Library

DIMOS relies on the ParmEd library for Amber file parsing. ParmEd provides:

| Capability | Description |
|------------|-------------|
| **File Parsing** | Reads `.prmtop` and `.inpcrd` formats |
| **Structure Manipulation** | Allows topology modifications |
| **Unit Handling** | Manages physical units and conversions |
| **Format Conversion** | Can convert between Amber/GROMACS/PDB formats |

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "External Library"
        PARMED["ParmEd Library"]
        RST7["parmed.amber.Rst7"]
        STRUCT["parmed.Structure"]
    end
    
    subgraph "DIMOS Components"
        AMBERFF["dimos.ff.AmberForceField"]
        COORDS["Position Tensors"]
    end
    
    PRMTOP[".prmtop Files"]
    INPCRD[".inpcrd Files"]
    
    PRMTOP --> PARMED
    INPCRD --> RST7
    
    PARMED --> AMBERFF
    RST7 --> COORDS
    
    STRUCT -.->|"Can generate"| PRMTOP
    STRUCT -.->|"Can generate"| INPCRD
```

### Unit Conversion

ParmEd handles unit conversions automatically. When extracting positions, always specify the desired unit:

```python
# Correct: Specify units explicitly
positions_angstrom = rst7_file.positions.value_in_unit(parmed.unit.angstrom)

# ParmEd also supports other units
positions_nm = rst7_file.positions.value_in_unit(parmed.unit.nanometer)
```

**Sources:** [benchmark/water/dimos_water.py:58-59]()

---

## Generating Amber Files

### Using ParmEd to Create Files

ParmEd structures can be saved to Amber format files:

```mermaid
graph TD
    SOURCE["Source:<br/>- OpenMM System<br/>- GROMACS files<br/>- PDB files"]
    
    PARMED_STRUCT["parmed.Structure<br/>or<br/>parmed.openmm.load_topology()"]
    
    SAVE_PRMTOP["structure.save()<br/>.prmtop"]
    
    SAVE_INPCRD["structure.save()<br/>.inpcrd"]
    
    PRMTOP_FILE[".prmtop File"]
    INPCRD_FILE[".inpcrd File"]
    
    SOURCE --> PARMED_STRUCT
    PARMED_STRUCT --> SAVE_PRMTOP
    PARMED_STRUCT --> SAVE_INPCRD
    
    SAVE_PRMTOP --> PRMTOP_FILE
    SAVE_INPCRD --> INPCRD_FILE
```

### Example: Generating Water Box Files

The water box generation script demonstrates file creation:

```python
# Create system using OpenMM tools
waterbox = mmtools.testsystems.WaterBox(
    box_edge=100*parmed.unit.angstrom,
    constrained=False
)

# Convert to ParmEd structure
structure = parmed.openmm.load_topology(
    waterbox.topology,
    waterbox.system,
    waterbox.positions
)

# Save to Amber format
structure.save('amber100.prmtop', overwrite=True)
structure.save('amber100.inpcrd', overwrite=True)
```

**Sources:** [benchmark/water/generate_water_box_amber.py:7-18]()

---

## Amber Format Advantages and Limitations

### Advantages

| Advantage | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| **Compact** | Binary format is space-efficient |
| **Complete** | Single `.prmtop` contains all force field data |
| **Widely Used** | Compatible with AMBER, OpenMM, and many tools |
| **Well-Documented** | Extensive documentation and examples available |

### Limitations

| Limitation | Description |
|------------|-------------|
| **Binary Format** | `.prmtop` not easily human-readable |
| **Fixed Precision** | Coordinate precision limited by format specification |
| **No Velocities in Basic Format** | Standard `.inpcrd` doesn't include velocities (`.rst7` does) |
| **Amber-Specific** | Primarily designed for AMBER force fields |

### Comparison with GROMACS Formats

| Feature | Amber (.prmtop/.inpcrd) | GROMACS (.top/.gro) |
|---------|-------------------------|---------------------|
| **Topology Format** | Binary/ASCII hybrid | Human-readable text |
| **Coordinate Format** | Fixed-width ASCII | Fixed-width ASCII |
| **Editability** | Difficult | Easy (text-based) |
| **Tool Support** | AMBER, OpenMM, ParmEd | GROMACS, OpenMM, ParmEd |
| **Force Field Flexibility** | Amber FF primarily | Multiple FF support |

---

## Usage in DIMOS Benchmarking

### Water System Benchmarks

The DIMOS benchmarking suite extensively uses Amber formats for water simulations:

```mermaid
graph TD
    GEN["generate_water_box_amber.py<br/>Generate Systems"]
    
    SIZES["Multiple Box Sizes:<br/>10-120 Å"]
    
    FILES["Amber Files:<br/>amber20.prmtop<br/>amber20.inpcrd<br/>..."]
    
    BENCH["dimos_water.py<br/>Benchmark Script"]
    
    PLATFORMS["Test on Platforms:<br/>- DIMOS (CPU/CUDA)<br/>- OpenMM<br/>- TorchMD"]
    
    GEN --> SIZES
    SIZES --> FILES
    FILES --> BENCH
    BENCH --> PLATFORMS
```

The benchmark loads systems across multiple sizes:

```python
# Parameterized by box size
box_size = int(sys.argv[3])

# Load corresponding files
rst7_file = parmed.amber.Rst7(f'amber{box_size}.inpcrd')
dimos_system = dimos.ff.AmberForceField(
    f'amber{box_size}.prmtop',
    cutoff=10,
    switch_distance=7.5,
    nonbonded_type=nonbonded,
    periodic=True,
    dtype=dtype_ff
)
```

This allows systematic performance testing across system sizes ranging from ~900 atoms (10 Å box) to ~165,000 atoms (120 Å box).

**Sources:** [benchmark/water/dimos_water.py:28, 58-61](), [benchmark/water/generate_water_box_amber.py:6-18]()

---

## Advanced: OpenMM Integration

### Loading Amber Files in OpenMM

DIMOS benchmarks also compare against OpenMM, which has native Amber format support:

```python
# OpenMM's native Amber loader
openmm_prmtop = mmapp.AmberPrmtopFile('amber100.prmtop')

# Create OpenMM system with parameters
openmm_system = openmm_prmtop.createSystem(
    removeCMMotion=False,
    constraints=None,
    rigidWater=False,
    nonbondedMethod=mmapp.forcefield.PME,
    nonbondedCutoff=10*mm.unit.angstrom,
    switchDistance=7.5*mm.unit.angstrom
)
```

This allows direct performance comparisons between DIMOS and OpenMM using identical input files.

**Sources:** [benchmark/water/dimos_water.py:79-86]()

---

## File Format Summary

### Quick Reference Table

| File Type | Extension | Contains | Load Method | DIMOS Use |
|-----------|-----------|----------|-------------|-----------|
| **Topology** | `.prmtop` | Force field parameters, connectivity | `dimos.ff.AmberForceField(path)` | System initialization |
| **Coordinates** | `.inpcrd`, `.rst7` | Atomic positions, box dimensions | `parmed.amber.Rst7(path)` | Initial positions |

### Typical File Sizes

For water systems (TIP3P model):

| Box Size | Atoms | .prmtop Size | .inpcrd Size |
|----------|-------|--------------|--------------|
| 20 Å | ~900 | ~50 KB | ~20 KB |
| 50 Å | ~14,000 | ~700 KB | ~300 KB |
| 100 Å | ~110,000 | ~5 MB | ~2 MB |

**Sources:** [benchmark/water/generate_water_box_amber.py:6-18]()

---

## Best Practices

### File Management

1. **Keep Topology and Coordinates Together**: Always maintain `.prmtop` and `.inpcrd` pairs with matching names
2. **Version Control**: Topology files should be version controlled; large coordinate files may be stored separately
3. **Backup Restart Files**: `.rst7` files from production runs should be backed up regularly
4. **Validate Loading**: Always verify system size matches expectations after loading

### Performance Considerations

1. **File I/O**: Amber file loading is fast but not instantaneous for large systems
2. **Precision**: Coordinate precision in `.inpcrd` is sufficient for most applications
3. **Periodic Boundaries**: Ensure box dimensions are correctly loaded for periodic simulations
4. **Unit Consistency**: Always explicitly specify units when extracting values from ParmEd

### Troubleshooting Common Issues

| Issue | Cause | Solution |
|-------|-------|----------|
| **Atom count mismatch** | `.prmtop` and `.inpcrd` from different systems | Verify files correspond to same system |
| **Missing box dimensions** | Non-periodic system or old format | Check file has box info line |
| **Unit errors** | Forgetting to specify units | Always use `.value_in_unit()` |
| **ParmEd import errors** | Missing dependency | Install with `pip install parmed` |

**Sources:** [benchmark/water/dimos_water.py:58-61]()

---

# Page: Developer Guide

# Developer Guide

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [.gitignore](.gitignore)
- [LICENSE](LICENSE)
- [dimos/__init__.py](dimos/__init__.py)

This guide provides technical information for developers who want to contribute to DIMOS, extend its functionality, or create derivative works. It covers the codebase architecture, module organization, design patterns, and extension points.

For setting up your development environment and running tests, see [Development Environment Setup](#8.2). For guidelines on creating derivative works under the academic license, see [Creating Derivative Works](#8.3). For understanding the module organization in detail, see [Project Structure and Architecture](#8.1).

---

## Architectural Philosophy

DIMOS is designed as a modular, PyTorch-based molecular dynamics framework with three core architectural principles:

1. **Modularity**: Components are loosely coupled and can be mixed and matched (e.g., different integrators, constraints, force fields)
2. **Differentiability**: All operations use PyTorch tensors, enabling automatic differentiation through the entire simulation
3. **Extensibility**: Clear extension points for adding new force fields, integrators, sampling methods, and analysis tools

The framework follows a layered architecture where high-level simulation orchestration depends on lower-level computational kernels, with a clear separation between physics algorithms and computational infrastructure.

**Sources**: [dimos/__init__.py:1-389](), high-level architecture diagrams

---

## Module Organization

The DIMOS codebase is organized into focused modules, each handling a specific aspect of molecular simulation. The following diagram shows the primary modules and their dependencies:

### Package Structure

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Core Modules"
        simulation["simulation.py<br/>MDSimulation, MCSimulation"]
        energy["energy.py<br/>Energy calculations"]
        integrators["integrators/<br/>Langevin, NoseHoover"]
        constraints["constraints.py<br/>CCMA, SETTLE"]
        barostats["barostats.py<br/>MC barostats"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Force Field Modules"
        ff["ff.py<br/>AmberForceField, GromacsForceField"]
        mlmm["mlmm.py<br/>MLMMsystem"]
        ml_integrations["mace_helper.py, orb_helper.py<br/>ML potential wrappers"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Infrastructure"
        constants["constants.py<br/>Unit systems, physical constants"]
        neighbor["neighbor_handling.py<br/>Neighbor lists"]
        utils["utils.py<br/>I/O, structure manipulation"]
        splines["splines.py<br/>Interpolation utilities"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Advanced Methods"
        metadynamics["advanced_methods/metadynamics.py<br/>Metadynamics engine"]
        replica_exchange["advanced_methods/replica_exchange.py<br/>Replica exchange"]
        distribution["distribution.py<br/>Probability distributions"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Long-Range"
        ewald["ewald.py<br/>Ewald summation, PME"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Monte Carlo"
        monte_carlo["monte_carlo.py<br/>MC move proposals"]
    end
    
    simulation --> integrators
    simulation --> constraints
    simulation --> barostats
    simulation --> energy
    
    energy --> ff
    energy --> neighbor
    energy --> ewald
    energy --> constants
    
    ff --> utils
    ff --> constants
    
    mlmm --> ff
    mlmm --> ml_integrations
    
    metadynamics --> simulation
    metadynamics --> splines
    replica_exchange --> simulation
    
    barostats --> monte_carlo
    barostats --> distribution
    
    integrators --> constants
```

**Sources**: [dimos/__init__.py:374-388]()

---

## Key Classes and Their Responsibilities

The following table summarizes the primary classes in DIMOS and their roles:

| Class/Module | File | Responsibility |
|--------------|------|----------------|
| `MDSimulation` | `simulation.py` | Orchestrates MD simulation loop with integrator, constraints, and optional barostat |
| `MCSimulation` | `simulation.py` | Orchestrates Monte Carlo simulations |
| `AmberForceField` | `ff.py` | Loads and evaluates Amber topology/parameter files |
| `GromacsForceField` | `ff.py` | Loads and evaluates GROMACS topology files |
| `MLMMsystem` | `mlmm.py` | Hybrid ML/MM system combining ML potentials with classical force fields |
| `LangevinIntegrator` | `integrators/langevin.py` | Langevin dynamics integration |
| `NoseHooverIntegrator` | `integrators/nosehoover.py` | Nosé-Hoover thermostat integration |
| `CCMA` | `constraints.py` | General holonomic constraint solver using CCMA algorithm |
| `SETTLE` | `constraints.py` | Fast water molecule constraint solver |
| `MCBarostat`, `MCAnisotropicBarostat` | `barostats.py` | Monte Carlo pressure control for NPT ensembles |
| `Metadynamics` | `advanced_methods/metadynamics.py` | Metadynamics enhanced sampling |
| `ReplicaExchange` | `advanced_methods/replica_exchange.py` | Temperature replica exchange implementation |
| `NeighborList` | `neighbor_handling.py` | Cell-list based neighbor list construction |

**Sources**: [dimos/__init__.py:374-388]()

---

## Core Simulation Flow

Understanding the simulation loop is essential for extending DIMOS. The following diagram shows the data flow and method calls during a typical MD simulation step:

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "MDSimulation.run()"
        init["initialize()<br/>positions, velocities, box"]
        loop_start["for step in range(n_steps)"]
        
        subgraph "Single Step"
            neighbor_check["if step % neighbor_update_freq"]
            neighbor_update["neighbor_list.update()"]
            force["compute_forces()<br/>from energy module"]
            apply_constraints_pos["constraints.apply_position()"]
            integrate["integrator.step()"]
            apply_constraints_vel["constraints.apply_velocity()"]
            barostat_check["if barostat and MC trial"]
            barostat_move["barostat.attempt_move()"]
        end
        
        output["write_trajectory()"]
        stats["compute_statistics()"]
    end
    
    init --> loop_start
    loop_start --> neighbor_check
    neighbor_check --> neighbor_update
    neighbor_update --> force
    neighbor_check --> force
    force --> apply_constraints_pos
    apply_constraints_pos --> integrate
    integrate --> apply_constraints_vel
    apply_constraints_vel --> barostat_check
    barostat_check --> barostat_move
    barostat_check --> output
    barostat_move --> output
    output --> stats
    stats --> loop_start
```

**Sources**: Inferred from simulation architecture diagrams and module structure

---

## Architectural Patterns

### 1. Unit System Management

DIMOS uses a centralized constant management system to ensure consistency across all calculations. The `constants.py` module provides:

```python
# Unit system initialization pattern
from dimos import constants
constants.init_constants_in_unit_system('kcal/mol')  # or 'kJ/mol' or 'lj'

# Access constants throughout codebase
coulomb_constant = constants.ONE_BY_4_PI_EPSILON_0
boltzmann = constants.BOLTZMANN
```

**Pattern**: All physical constants are accessed through module-level variables in `constants.py`. The `init_constants_in_unit_system()` function sets these values based on the chosen unit convention (Amber, GROMACS, or reduced units). This ensures all components use consistent units without passing unit information through every function call.

**Sources**: [dimos/__init__.py:376](), constants module reference from diagrams

---

### 2. Force Field Plugin Architecture

Force fields in DIMOS follow an interface pattern where different implementations provide the same core methods:

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Force Field Interface Pattern"
        ff_interface["Force Field Methods<br/>compute_energy()<br/>compute_forces()<br/>get_system_info()"]
        
        amber_impl["AmberForceField<br/>Reads .prmtop/.inpcrd<br/>Classical MM terms"]
        gromacs_impl["GromacsForceField<br/>Reads .gro/.top<br/>Classical MM terms"]
        ml_wrapper["as_mace_system()<br/>as_orb_system()<br/>Wraps with ML calculator"]
        hybrid["MLMMsystem<br/>Combines ML + MM"]
    end
    
    ff_interface --> amber_impl
    ff_interface --> gromacs_impl
    
    amber_impl --> ml_wrapper
    gromacs_impl --> ml_wrapper
    
    ml_wrapper --> hybrid
    amber_impl --> hybrid
```

**Pattern**: Force field classes implement a common interface for energy/force computation. Conversion functions (`as_mace_system()`, `as_orb_system()`) wrap existing force fields with ML calculators. This allows seamless substitution and hybrid combinations.

**Extension Point**: To add a new force field:
1. Implement `compute_energy()` and `compute_forces()` methods returning tensors
2. Provide `get_system_info()` returning atom counts, masses, box dimensions
3. Optionally support conversion to ML-based systems

**Sources**: [dimos/__init__.py:379](), [dimos/__init__.py:381](), force field architecture diagram

---

### 3. Integrator Interface

Integrators follow a strategy pattern where different integration schemes implement a common interface:

```python
# Integrator interface pattern
class IntegratorBase:
    def step(self, positions, velocities, forces, dt):
        """Single integration step, returns updated positions/velocities"""
        pass
```

**Extension Point**: To implement a new integrator:
1. Create a class in the `integrators/` directory
2. Implement `step()` method taking positions, velocities, forces, timestep
3. Use `constants.FS_TO_INTERNAL` for time unit conversion
4. Return updated positions and velocities as PyTorch tensors
5. Import in `integrators/__init__.py`

**Sources**: [dimos/__init__.py:380](), integrator module structure

---

### 4. Constraint Algorithm Plugin

Constraints use a plugin pattern where specific algorithms can be swapped:

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Constraint System"
        constraint_call["MDSimulation calls<br/>apply_position_constraints()<br/>apply_velocity_constraints()"]
        
        ccma["CCMA<br/>General holonomic constraints<br/>Works on any constraint set"]
        settle["SETTLE<br/>Specialized for water<br/>Analytical solution"]
        none["NoConstraints<br/>Pass-through"]
    end
    
    constraint_call --> ccma
    constraint_call --> settle
    constraint_call --> none
```

**Extension Point**: To add a new constraint algorithm:
1. Implement `apply_position_constraints(positions, velocities, ...)` 
2. Implement `apply_velocity_constraints(positions, velocities, ...)`
3. Handle periodic boundary conditions if applicable
4. Ensure constraint satisfaction to specified tolerance

**Sources**: [dimos/__init__.py:375](), constraints module

---

## Extension Points for Advanced Sampling

### Collective Variables

Metadynamics uses an abstract `CollectiveVariable` interface:

```python
# CV interface pattern
class CollectiveVariable:
    def compute(self, positions, box):
        """Compute CV value and derivatives"""
        return cv_value, cv_derivatives
```

**Extension Point**: To add a new collective variable:
1. Inherit from `CollectiveVariable` base class
2. Implement `compute()` returning CV value and gradients w.r.t. positions
3. Specify periodicity bounds if CV is periodic (e.g., dihedral angles)
4. Register with metadynamics engine

**Sources**: [dimos/__init__.py:387](), advanced_methods module, metadynamics diagram

---

### Distribution Classes for Sampling

The `distribution.py` module provides probability distribution classes used in advanced sampling:

| Class | Purpose | Use Case |
|-------|---------|----------|
| `ContinuousDistribution` | Standard normal distribution | Langevin noise, MC proposals |
| `DiscretizedDistribution` | Histogram-based distribution | Bias potential representation |
| `TruncatedNormalDistribution` | Bounded normal distribution | Constrained sampling |
| `FoldedNormalDistribution` | Periodic distribution | Angular sampling |

**Extension Point**: Add new distributions by implementing `sample()` and `log_prob()` methods.

**Sources**: [dimos/__init__.py:387](), distribution module

---

## PyTorch Integration and Differentiability

DIMOS is built on PyTorch, which provides several key capabilities:

### Automatic Differentiation

All force calculations naturally support `torch.autograd`:

```python
# Energy is differentiable
positions.requires_grad_(True)
energy = forcefield.compute_energy(positions, box)
forces = -torch.autograd.grad(energy.sum(), positions)[0]
```

### JIT Compilation

DIMOS supports `torch.compile()` for performance:

```python
# Compilation pattern used in benchmarks
compiled_step = torch.compile(simulation_step_function)
```

**Note**: Compilation adds overhead on first call but accelerates subsequent iterations. Best for long simulations (>1000 steps).

**Sources**: Benchmark files show compilation patterns, PyTorch architecture

---

## Working with Neighbor Lists

The `neighbor_handling.py` module provides efficient neighbor list construction using cell lists:

```python
# Neighbor list usage pattern
from dimos import NeighborList

neighbor_list = NeighborList(cutoff=12.0, skin=2.0)
neighbors = neighbor_list.compute(positions, box)
# neighbors is sparse tensor or pair list
```

**Key Parameters**:
- `cutoff`: Interaction cutoff distance
- `skin`: Extra distance for neighbor list buffering (reduces rebuild frequency)
- Update frequency: Typically every 10-20 steps depending on temperature

**Extension Point**: Custom neighbor list implementations can be added by implementing the same interface.

**Sources**: [dimos/__init__.py:383](), neighbor_handling module

---

## File I/O and Structure Manipulation

The `utils.py` module provides functions for reading/writing molecular structure files:

```python
# Common I/O patterns
from dimos.utils import read_gromacs_files, write_pdb

positions, box, topology = read_gromacs_files('system.gro', 'system.top')
write_pdb(positions, box, topology, 'output.pdb')
```

**Supported Formats**:
- Input: `.gro`, `.top`, `.prmtop`, `.inpcrd`, `.pdb`
- Output: `.pdb`, `.xtc` (trajectory)

**Extension Point**: Add new file format parsers by implementing reader functions in `utils.py`.

**Sources**: [dimos/__init__.py:386](), utils module

---

## Testing and Validation

DIMOS includes comprehensive benchmarking infrastructure for validation:

### Test Systems

Located in `benchmarks/`:
- `benchmark_proteins.py`: Protein system benchmarks (ala2, DHFR, Trp-cage)
- `dimos_water.py`: Classical water benchmarks
- `dimos_water_ml.py`: ML potential water benchmarks

### Benchmark Patterns

```python
# Typical benchmark structure
1. Load system from files
2. Initialize force field with specific parameters
3. Run simulation with/without compilation
4. Compare against reference (OpenMM, TorchMD)
5. Report timing and energy conservation
```

**Extension Point**: Add new benchmarks by following the existing patterns in the `benchmarks/` directory.

**Sources**: Benchmark suite diagram, benchmark file references

## Code Style and Conventions

### Naming Conventions

- **Classes**: `PascalCase` (e.g., `LangevinIntegrator`, `AmberForceField`)
- **Functions**: `snake_case` (e.g., `compute_energy`, `apply_constraints`)
- **Constants**: `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` (e.g., `BOLTZMANN`, `ONE_BY_4_PI_EPSILON_0`)
- **Private methods**: Prefix with `_` (e.g., `_update_internal_state`)

### Documentation

- All public functions and classes should have docstrings
- Include parameter types and return types
- Note units for physical quantities
- Reference papers for algorithms when applicable

### License Headers

All source files must include the NEC Software Library Academic Use License header as shown in [dimos/__init__.py:1-372](). This is required for both core code and derivative works.

**Sources**: [dimos/__init__.py:1-389](), [LICENSE:1-372]()

---

## Key Design Decisions

### Why PyTorch?

1. **Automatic differentiation**: Enables ML/MM hybrid approaches and force field parameterization
2. **GPU acceleration**: Native CUDA support without custom kernels
3. **Ecosystem integration**: Easy integration with ML frameworks (MACE, ORB)
4. **JIT compilation**: `torch.compile()` provides performance competitive with C++

### Why Not OpenMM Integration?

DIMOS is a standalone implementation rather than wrapping OpenMM because:
1. Full control over differentiability
2. Simpler integration with ML potentials
3. Easier modification and extension for research
4. Transparent implementation for educational purposes

OpenMM is used as a validation reference in benchmarks but not as a backend.

**Sources**: Architecture philosophy from diagrams and README context

# Page: Project Structure and Architecture

# Project Structure and Architecture

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [.gitignore](.gitignore)
- [dimos/__init__.py](dimos/__init__.py)

## Purpose and Scope

This document describes the organizational structure of the DIMOS codebase, including the module hierarchy, package organization, and key architectural patterns. It provides a map from conceptual components to actual code entities (classes, modules, functions) to help developers navigate and extend the framework.

For information about setting up a development environment and running tests, see [Development Environment Setup](#8.2). For guidelines on creating derivative works, see [Creating Derivative Works](#8.3).

## Directory Structure Overview

The DIMOS repository follows a standard Python package structure with clear separation between core library code, benchmarking scripts, and test systems:

```
DIMOS/
├── dimos/                    # Core library package
│   ├── __init__.py          # Package exports and license
│   ├── barostats.py         # Pressure control implementations
│   ├── constraints.py       # Molecular constraint algorithms
│   ├── constants.py         # Physical constants and unit systems
│   ├── energy.py            # Energy calculation functions
│   ├── ewald.py             # Long-range electrostatics
│   ├── ff.py                # Force field implementations
│   ├── integrators.py       # Time integration schemes
│   ├── mlmm.py              # Hybrid ML/MM systems
│   ├── monte_carlo.py       # Monte Carlo simulation engine
│   ├── neighbor_handling.py # Neighbor list management
│   ├── simulation.py        # Molecular dynamics simulation engine
│   ├── splines.py           # Interpolation utilities
│   ├── utils.py             # General utilities
│   └── distribution.py      # Probability distributions
├── advanced_methods/         # Enhanced sampling techniques
│   ├── metadynamics.py      # Metadynamics implementation
│   └── replica_exchange.py  # Replica exchange implementation
├── benchmarking/            # Performance benchmarking scripts
│   ├── benchmark_proteins.py
│   ├── dimos_water.py
│   └── dimos_water_ml.py
└── test_systems/            # Molecular system files (.gro, .top, etc.)
```

The [`.gitignore:1-181`]() file specifies standard Python exclusions plus project-specific patterns for data files, models, and trajectory outputs.

**Sources:** `.gitignore`, repository structure from high-level diagrams

## Core Package Organization

The `dimos` package is structured as a flat module hierarchy where each module has a focused responsibility. The main package initialization file [`dimos/__init__.py:374-388`]() exports all public APIs through star imports:

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "dimos Package"
        INIT["__init__.py<br/>Package Entry Point"]
        
        BAROSTATS["barostats.py<br/>MC pressure control"]
        CONSTRAINTS["constraints.py<br/>CCMA, SETTLE algorithms"]
        CONSTANTS["constants.py<br/>Unit system management"]
        ENERGY["energy.py<br/>Force field calculations"]
        EWALD["ewald.py<br/>Long-range electrostatics"]
        FF["ff.py<br/>AmberForceField, GromacsForceField"]
        INTEGRATORS["integrators.py<br/>Langevin, NoseHoover"]
        MLMM["mlmm.py<br/>MLMMsystem, as_mace_system, as_orb_system"]
        MC["monte_carlo.py<br/>MCSimulation"]
        NEIGHBOR["neighbor_handling.py<br/>Neighbor list updates"]
        SIMULATION["simulation.py<br/>MDSimulation"]
        SPLINES["splines.py<br/>Interpolation utilities"]
        UTILS["utils.py<br/>Helper functions"]
        DIST["distribution.py<br/>Sampling distributions"]
    end
    
    INIT --> BAROSTATS
    INIT --> CONSTRAINTS
    INIT --> CONSTANTS
    INIT --> ENERGY
    INIT --> EWALD
    INIT --> FF
    INIT --> INTEGRATORS

```

**Sources:** `dimos/__init__.py:374-388`

## Module Responsibilities and Key Classes

The following table maps each core module to its primary classes, functions, and responsibilities:

| Module | Key Entities | Primary Responsibility |
|--------|-------------|----------------------|
| `simulation.py` | `MDSimulation` | Main molecular dynamics simulation loop, trajectory management, statistics collection |
| `monte_carlo.py` | `MCSimulation` | Monte Carlo simulation engine for configurational sampling |
| `energy.py` | `compute_*_energy` functions | Bonded and nonbonded energy calculations, force computation |
| `ff.py` | `AmberForceField`, `GromacsForceField` | Force field parameter loading and management from topology files |
| `integrators.py` | `LangevinIntegrator`, `NoseHooverIntegrator` | Time integration schemes for MD trajectories |
| `constraints.py` | `CCMA`, `SETTLE` | Constraint algorithms for fixed bond lengths and rigid water |
| `barostats.py` | `MonteCarloIsotropicBarostat`, `MonteCarloAnisotropicBarostat` | NPT ensemble pressure control via volume moves |
| `ewald.py` | `compute_ewald_energy`, `compute_pme_energy` | Long-range electrostatic interactions |
| `neighbor_handling.py` | `update_neighbor_list` | Efficient neighbor list construction and updates |
| `constants.py` | `init_constants_in_unit_system`, physical constants | Unit system initialization (Amber, GROMACS, reduced) |
| `mlmm.py` | `MLMMsystem`, `as_mace_system`, `as_orb_system` | ML potential integration and hybrid ML/MM setup |
| `splines.py` | `Spline1D`, `Spline2D` | Interpolation for tabulated potentials |
| `distribution.py` | `ContinuousDistribution`, `DiscretizedDistribution` | Probability distributions for enhanced sampling |
| `utils.py` | Helper functions | File I/O, coordinate transformations, utilities |

**Sources:** `dimos/__init__.py:374-388`, high-level system architecture diagram

## Architectural Pattern: Modular Simulation Engine

DIMOS follows a **modular composition pattern** where the simulation engine (`MDSimulation` or `MCSimulation`) orchestrates loosely-coupled components:

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Simulation Initialization"
        FF_INPUT["Force Field Input<br/>.prmtop/.inpcrd or .gro/.top"]
        FF_CLASS["AmberForceField or<br/>GromacsForceField"]
        ML_CONVERT["Optional ML Conversion<br/>as_mace_system, as_orb_system"]
        HYBRID_CREATE["Optional Hybrid<br/>MLMMsystem"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Component Configuration"
        INT_CONFIG["Integrator<br/>LangevinIntegrator,<br/>NoseHooverIntegrator"]
        CONST_CONFIG["Constraints<br/>CCMA, SETTLE"]
        BARO_CONFIG["Barostat (optional)<br/>MonteCarloIsotropicBarostat"]
        NEIGHBOR_CONFIG["Neighbor List<br/>update_neighbor_list"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Simulation Engine"
        SIM["MDSimulation or<br/>MCSimulation"]
        LOOP["Simulation Loop<br/>run() method"]
    end
    
    FF_INPUT --> FF_CLASS
    FF_CLASS --> ML_CONVERT
    FF_CLASS --> HYBRID_CREATE
    ML_CONVERT --> HYBRID_CREATE
    
    FF_CLASS --> SIM
    ML_CONVERT --> SIM
    HYBRID_CREATE --> SIM
    
    INT_CONFIG --> SIM
    CONST_CONFIG --> SIM
    BARO_CONFIG --> SIM
    NEIGHBOR_CONFIG --> SIM
    
    SIM --> LOOP
```

This design allows developers to:
- Swap integrators without modifying energy calculations
- Enable/disable constraints independently
- Add new force field types by implementing the force field interface
- Mix classical and ML potentials through the hybrid system

**Sources:** High-level system architecture diagram (Diagram 1), force field architecture diagram (Diagram 2)

## Dependency Graph: Core Module Interactions

The following diagram shows the dependency relationships between core modules. Arrows indicate "imports from" or "depends on":

```mermaid
graph LR
    SIMULATION["simulation.py"]
    MC["monte_carlo.py"]
    ENERGY["energy.py"]
    FF["ff.py"]
    INT["integrators.py"]
    CONST["constraints.py"]
    BARO["barostats.py"]
    EWALD["ewald.py"]
    NEIGHBOR["neighbor_handling.py"]
    CONSTANTS["constants.py"]
    MLMM["mlmm.py"]
    SPLINES["splines.py"]
    UTILS["utils.py"]
    DIST["distribution.py"]
    
    SIMULATION --> ENERGY
    SIMULATION --> INT
    SIMULATION --> CONST
    SIMULATION --> BARO
    SIMULATION --> NEIGHBOR
    SIMULATION --> UTILS
    
    MC --> BARO
    MC --> ENERGY
    MC --> UTILS
    
    ENERGY --> EWALD
    ENERGY --> NEIGHBOR
    ENERGY --> CONSTANTS
    ENERGY --> UTILS
    
    FF --> UTILS
    FF --> CONSTANTS
    
    MLMM --> FF
    MLMM --> ENERGY
    
    INT --> CONSTANTS
    INT --> DIST
    
    BARO --> CONSTANTS
    BARO --> DIST
    
    EWALD --> CONSTANTS
    
    SPLINES --> UTILS
    
    CONST --> CONSTANTS
```

**Key architectural observations:**

1. **`constants.py` is a foundation module** - It has no dependencies and is used by `energy.py`, `ewald.py`, `integrators.py`, `barostats.py`, and `constraints.py` to ensure consistent physical constants.

2. **`energy.py` is a central computation hub** - It depends on `ewald.py` for long-range interactions, `neighbor_handling.py` for efficiency, and provides force calculations to both `simulation.py` and `monte_carlo.py`.

3. **`simulation.py` orchestrates everything** - The MD simulation engine composes energy calculations, integrators, constraints, barostats, and neighbor lists.

4. **`mlmm.py` bridges classical and ML** - It depends on `ff.py` for classical force field infrastructure and provides conversion functions to ML-based systems.

**Sources:** `dimos/__init__.py:374-388`, inferred from module responsibilities

## Advanced Methods Subsystem

Enhanced sampling methods are implemented as a separate subsystem that extends the core simulation engine:

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "advanced_methods Package"
        META["metadynamics.py"]
        REPEX["replica_exchange.py"]
        
        subgraph "Metadynamics Components"
            CV["CollectiveVariable<br/>(abstract base)"]
            DIHEDRAL_CV["DihedralCV"]
            TAB_FORCE["TabulatedCVForce"]
            GAUSSIAN["Gaussian hills"]
        end
        
        subgraph "Replica Exchange Components"
            METRO["Metropolis criterion"]
            TEMP_SWAP["Temperature swapping"]
            VEL_SCALE["Velocity rescaling"]
        end
        
        META --> CV
        META --> DIHEDRAL_CV
        META --> TAB_FORCE
        META --> GAUSSIAN
        
        REPEX --> METRO
        REPEX --> TEMP_SWAP
        REPEX --> VEL_SCALE
    end
    
    SIM_BASE["simulation.py<br/>MDSimulation"]
    SPLINES_MOD["splines.py<br/>Spline1D, Spline2D"]
    
    META --> SIM_BASE
    META --> SPLINES_MOD
    REPEX --> SIM_BASE
```

The `advanced_methods` package provides experimental features that integrate with the base `MDSimulation` class. For detailed information on these methods, see [Metadynamics](#5.1) and [Replica Exchange and Parallel Tempering](#5.2).

**Sources:** High-level system architecture diagram (Diagram 4), advanced methods subsystem description

Benchmarking scripts are located in the `benchmarking/` directory and are not part of the core package. They demonstrate usage patterns and provide performance comparisons. For details on running benchmarks, see [Protein Benchmark Systems](#6.1) and [Water System Benchmarks](#6.2).

**Sources:** High-level system architecture diagram (Diagram 3), benchmarking ecosystem diagram

## Key Architectural Patterns

### 1. PyTorch-First Design

All computation is implemented using PyTorch tensors and operations, enabling:
- **GPU acceleration**: Automatic CUDA support when tensors are on GPU
- **Automatic differentiation**: Full gradient tracking through force calculations
- **JIT compilation**: `torch.compile` optimization of simulation loops and energy functions

### 2. Unit System Abstraction

The [`constants.py`]() module implements a **global state pattern** for unit system management:

```mermaid
graph LR
    USER["User calls<br/>init_constants_in_unit_system"]
    CHOICE["Unit system choice:<br/>'kcal/mol', 'kJ/mol', 'lj'"]
    INIT["Module-level globals<br/>set in constants.py"]
    USAGE["All modules import<br/>from dimos.constants"]
    
    USER --> CHOICE
    CHOICE --> INIT
    INIT --> USAGE
```

This ensures consistency across all calculations. See [Unit Systems and Physical Constants](#2.3) for details on available unit systems.

### 3. Force Field Interface Pattern

Force field classes (`AmberForceField`, `GromacsForceField`) provide a **factory pattern** for creating simulation systems:

- Load topology and coordinate files
- Parse force field parameters
- Provide methods to compute energies and forces
- Can be converted to ML-based systems via `as_mace_system()` or `as_orb_system()`

This abstraction allows swapping force fields without changing simulation code. See [Force Field Systems](#4) for comprehensive coverage.

### 4. Constraint Algorithm Strategy Pattern

The constraint system uses a **strategy pattern** where different constraint algorithms implement the same interface but use different mathematical approaches:

| Class | Algorithm | Use Case |
|-------|-----------|----------|
| `CCMA` | Cascading Coordinate Method | General holonomic constraints |
| `SETTLE` | Analytical solution | Rigid water molecules (optimized) |

Constraints are applied in two stages within the integration loop: position constraints after force calculation, and velocity constraints after integration. See [Molecular Constraints](#3.3) for implementation details.

### 5. Neighbor List Optimization

The [`neighbor_handling.py`]() module implements a **caching strategy** to avoid recomputing pairwise distances every step:

- Maintain a neighbor list with a buffer distance (`skin_distance`)
- Only update when atoms move beyond the buffer
- Reduce computational complexity from O(N²) to O(N) for most steps

**Sources:** High-level system architecture diagram (Diagram 5), inferred from module organization

## Extension Points for Developers

DIMOS provides several well-defined extension points:

### Adding New Integrators

Implement a new class in `integrators.py` with a `step()` method that updates positions and velocities. Must respect the constraint interface if enabled.

### Adding New Force Field Types

Create a new force field class in `ff.py` that:
- Loads system parameters from files
- Provides energy and force calculation methods
- Maintains parameter tensors (bonds, angles, charges, etc.)

### Adding New Collective Variables for Metadynamics

Subclass `CollectiveVariable` in `advanced_methods/metadynamics.py` and implement:
- `compute()`: Calculate CV value from coordinates
- `get_gradient()`: Compute derivative with respect to positions

### Adding New ML Potential Integrations

Add conversion functions in `mlmm.py` following the pattern of `as_mace_system()` and `as_orb_system()`:
- Accept a classical force field object
- Return a system compatible with the simulation engine
- Handle atom type mappings and unit conversions

**Sources:** High-level system architecture and inferred from modular design patterns

## Data Flow in a Typical Simulation

The following sequence shows how data flows through the system during initialization and execution:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant FF as "AmberForceField/<br/>GromacsForceField"
    participant Sim as "MDSimulation"
    participant Int as "Integrator"
    participant Energy as "energy.py"
    participant Const as "Constraints"
    participant Neigh as "Neighbor List"
    
    User->>FF: Load topology (.prmtop/.top)
    User->>FF: Load coordinates (.inpcrd/.gro)
    User->>Sim: Create MDSimulation(ff, integrator, ...)
    User->>Sim: run(n_steps)
    
    loop Each Simulation Step
        Sim->>Neigh: Check if update needed
        Neigh-->>Sim: Updated neighbor list
        Sim->>Energy: compute_energy(positions, box)
        Energy-->>Sim: energy, forces
        Sim->>Const: apply_position_constraints(positions)
        Const-->>Sim: constrained_positions
        Sim->>Int: step(positions, velocities, forces)
        Int-->>Sim: new_positions, new_velocities
        Sim->>Const: apply_velocity_constraints(velocities)
        Const-->>Sim: constrained_velocities
    end
    
    Sim-->>User: Trajectory, statistics
```

**Sources:** High-level system architecture diagram (Diagram 5), core simulation engine data flow

## Build and Distribution Structure

The project follows standard Python packaging conventions:

- **Package definition**: `setup.py` or `pyproject.toml` (not shown in provided files, but standard practice)
- **License inclusion**: Full academic use license in [`dimos/__init__.py:1-371`]()
- **Namespace management**: All public APIs exported via [`dimos/__init__.py:374-388`]()
- **Git exclusions**: Standard Python patterns in [`.gitignore:1-181`]()

The flat module structure (no deep nesting) simplifies imports and makes the API surface obvious. All core functionality is accessible via `from dimos import *` or selective imports like `from dimos import MDSimulation, AmberForceField`.

**Sources:** `dimos/__init__.py:1-389`, `.gitignore:1-181`

---

This architecture supports DIMOS's goals of being a differentiable, flexible, and performant molecular dynamics framework while maintaining clear separation of concerns and extensibility for research applications.

# Development Environment Setup

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

## Purpose and Scope

This page describes how to configure a development environment for contributing to DIMOS. It covers cloning the repository, installing dependencies (including optional packages for ML potentials and testing), running the test suite, and setting up development tools.

For information about the overall project structure and module organization, see [Project Structure and Architecture](#8.1). For guidelines on creating derivative works under the academic license, see [Creating Derivative Works](#8.3).

**Sources:** README.md:1-55

---

## Prerequisites

DIMOS requires Python 3.8 or later and depends on PyTorch as its core computational backend. Before setting up the development environment, ensure you have:

- Python 3.8+
- Git for version control
- A CUDA-capable GPU (optional, but recommended for performance testing)

**Sources:** README.md:26-55

---

## Repository Structure and Ignored Files

The repository uses a standard Python package layout with specific patterns for ignored files that help maintain a clean development environment.

### Ignored File Categories

The `.gitignore` configuration excludes several categories of files from version control:

| Category | Patterns | Purpose |
|----------|----------|---------|
| Python bytecode | `__pycache__/`, `*.py[cod]`, `*$py.class` | Compiled Python files |
| Distribution | `build/`, `dist/`, `*.egg-info/` | Package build artifacts |
| Testing | `.pytest_cache/`, `.coverage`, `htmlcov/` | Test execution artifacts |
| Virtual environments | `.venv`, `venv/`, `ENV/` | Isolated Python environments |
| IDE configurations | `.vscode/`, `.idea/`, `*.code-workspace` | Editor-specific settings |
| Data files | `*.pt`, `*.npy`, `*.h5`, `*.pkl`, `*.csv` | Model checkpoints and datasets |
| Trajectory files | `*.pdb`, `*.dat` | Simulation outputs |
| HPC outputs | `slurm*.out` | Batch job logs |

**Sources:** .gitignore:1-181

---

## Installation Methods

### Standard User Installation

For users who want to use DIMOS without modifying the source code:

```bash
pip install dimos-torch
```

This installs the package from PyPI with core dependencies only.

**Sources:** README.md:28-31

### Development Installation

For contributors who need to modify and test the codebase:

```mermaid
graph TD
    A["Clone Repository"] --> B["Navigate to Directory"]
    B --> C["Install Base Package"]
    C --> D{"Optional Dependencies?"}
    D -->|"Yes"| E["Install with Extras"]
    D -->|"No"| F["Basic Development Setup"]
    E --> G["Verify Installation"]
    F --> G
    G --> H["Run Tests"]
    
    subgraph "Commands"
        I["git clone https://github.com/nec-research/dimos.git"]
        J["cd dimos"]
        K["python -m pip install -e ."]
        L["python -m pip install -e '.[dev,mmtools,mace,orb]'"]
    end
    
    A -.-> I
    B -.-> J
    C -.-> K
    E -.-> L
```

**Diagram: Development Installation Workflow**

#### Clone the Repository

```bash
git clone https://github.com/nec-research/dimos.git
cd dimos
```

#### Install in Editable Mode

The editable installation (`-e` flag) creates a link to the source directory, allowing code changes to take effect immediately without reinstallation:

```bash
python -m pip install -e .
```

For full development capabilities with all optional dependencies:

```bash
python -m pip install -e '.[dev,mmtools,mace,orb]'
```

**Sources:** README.md:33-39

### Dependency Group Purposes

| Group | Purpose | Key Packages |
|-------|---------|--------------|
| `dev` | Testing, code formatting, linting | pytest, pytest-cov, black, flake8 |
| `mmtools` | Parsing Amber/GROMACS files | ParmEd, mdtraj |
| `mace` | MACE machine learning potential | mace-torch, e3nn |
| `orb` | ORB machine learning potential | orb-models |

## Test Platform Dependencies

For running benchmark comparisons against other MD engines, additional test dependencies are required.

### TorchMD Installation

The benchmarking suite includes comparisons with TorchMD (see [Platform Comparison and Performance](#6.3)). To install TorchMD without its proprietary `moleculekit` dependency:

```bash
pip install torchmd scipy networkx pandas tqdm pyyaml --no-deps
```

The `--no-deps` flag prevents installation of moleculekit, which is not required for the DIMOS benchmark workflows.

**Sources:** README.md:41-44

## Testing Infrastructure

### Running Tests

The project uses pytest as its testing framework. Test artifacts are automatically excluded from version control.

```mermaid
graph LR

    end

    DISCOVER --> EXECUTE
    EXECUTE --> REPORT
    
    EXECUTE --> CACHE
    EXECUTE --> COV
    EXECUTE --> HTML
    EXECUTE --> XML
    
    REPORT --> PASS
    REPORT --> FAIL
    REPORT --> SKIP
```

**Diagram: Testing Infrastructure and Artifact Management**

### Test Commands

```bash
# Run all tests
pytest

# Run tests with coverage report
pytest --cov=dimos --cov-report=html

# Run specific test module
pytest tests/test_energy.py

# Run tests verbosely
pytest -v
```

### Test Artifacts

The following test-related files and directories are excluded from version control:

- `.pytest_cache/` - Pytest cache directory
- `.coverage` - Coverage data file
- `htmlcov/` - HTML coverage report
- `coverage.xml` - XML coverage report (for CI/CD)
- `.hypothesis/` - Hypothesis testing framework cache

**Sources:** .gitignore:40-52, README.md:37-39

- `*.code-workspace` - Personal workspace configurations
- `.vscode/` in subdirectories

- `.idea/` directory

## Working with Data Files

The development environment automatically excludes large data files from version control to keep the repository size manageable:

**Model Files:**
- `*.pt` - PyTorch model checkpoints
- `*.h5`, `*.h5ad` - HDF5 data files
- `*.pkl` - Python pickle files
- `*.tar`, `*.tar.gz` - Compressed archives

**Simulation Data:**
- `*.npy`, `*.npz` - NumPy arrays
- `*.csv` - Tabular data
- `*.pdb` - Protein Data Bank files (except reference structures)
- `*.dat` - Generic data files

**Images and Documents:**
- `*.png`, `*.svg`, `*.gif`, `*.jpg` - Image files
- `*.pdf` - PDF documents

For developers working on HPC clusters, SLURM job output files are automatically excluded:

```bash
# Pattern matched by .gitignore

```

This prevents cluttering the repository with job log files when running benchmarks or large-scale simulations on compute clusters.

## Verification and Troubleshooting

### Verifying Installation

After installation, verify the setup by importing the package and checking available modules:

```python
import dimos

# Check core functionality
print(dimos.__version__)

# Verify force field modules
from dimos import AmberForceField
from dimos import GromacsForceField

# Verify integrators
from dimos import LangevinDynamics
from dimos import NoseHooverDynamics

# Check optional ML modules (if installed)
try:
    from dimos import as_mace_system
    print("MACE support available")
except ImportError:
    print("MACE not installed")

try:
    from dimos import as_orb_system
    print("ORB support available")
except ImportError:
    print("ORB not installed")
```

### Common Installation Issues

| Issue | Likely Cause | Solution |
|-------|--------------|----------|
| Import errors for ML potentials | Missing optional dependencies | Install with `pip install -e '.[mace,orb]'` |
| Test failures | Missing test dependencies | Install with `pip install -e '.[dev]'` |
| TorchMD comparison errors | Moleculekit dependency | Install with `--no-deps` flag as shown |
| CUDA errors | PyTorch CUDA version mismatch | Reinstall PyTorch with correct CUDA version |

**Sources:** README.md:48-54

---

## Environment Configuration Files

### Configuration File Patterns

The repository includes several configuration patterns that are excluded from version control:

**Environment Files:**
- `.env` - Environment variables
- `.autoenv` - Automatic environment activation
- `configs/local/default.yaml` - Local configuration overrides

**Python Environment:**
- `.python-version` - pyenv Python version specification
- `ipython_config.py` - IPython configuration
- `profile_default/` - IPython profile directory

These exclusions allow developers to maintain local configurations without affecting the shared codebase.

**Sources:** .gitignore:85-92, 143-148

## Getting Started with Development

### Minimal Setup Example

For a minimal development setup that allows running the core test suite:

```bash
# 1. Clone repository
git clone https://github.com/nec-research/dimos.git
cd dimos

# 2. Create virtual environment
python -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate

# 3. Install with dev dependencies
python -m pip install -e '.[dev,mmtools]'

# 4. Run tests to verify setup
pytest
```

### Full Setup Example

For a complete development environment with all optional features:

```bash
# 1. Clone repository
git clone https://github.com/nec-research/dimos.git
cd dimos

# 2. Create virtual environment
python -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate

# 3. Install all optional dependencies
python -m pip install -e '.[dev,mmtools,mace,orb]'

# 4. Install test platform dependencies
pip install torchmd scipy networkx pandas tqdm pyyaml --no-deps

# 5. Run full test suite
pytest -v

# 6. Run benchmark suite (optional)
python benchmarks/benchmark_proteins.py
```

**Sources:** README.md:33-54

---

## Summary

This page covered the essential steps for setting up a DIMOS development environment:

1. **Installation**: Editable installation with optional dependency groups
2. **Dependencies**: Core, dev tools, molecular mechanics tools, and ML potentials
3. **Testing**: pytest infrastructure and test artifact management
4. **IDE Support**: VS Code and JetBrains IDE configurations
5. **Virtual Environments**: Isolation of project dependencies
6. **Data Management**: Exclusion patterns for large files and simulation outputs
7. **HPC Integration**: SLURM job output handling

Developers should install at minimum the `[dev]` and `[mmtools]` extras to access the full development workflow. The `[mace]` and `[orb]` extras are required for testing ML potential functionality.

**Sources:** README.md:1-55, .gitignore:1-181

# Creating Derivative Works

<details>

## Purpose and Scope

This document provides technical and legal guidance for creating derivative works of the DIMOS software under the NEC Software Library Academic Use License. It covers ownership rights, mandatory compliance requirements, source code provision procedures, attribution requirements, and practical development workflows.

For general license terms and permitted uses, see [License and Academic Use Terms](#1.3). For development environment setup and contribution guidelines, see [Development Environment Setup](#8.2).

**Sources:** [LICENSE:1-372](), [dimos/__init__.py:1-372]()

---

## Definition of Derivative Works

Under the license terms, a **Derivative Work** is defined as any of the following:

| Category | Definition | Examples |
|----------|------------|----------|
| **Modifications** | Changes to existing DIMOS source code | Bug fixes, performance improvements, algorithm changes |
| **Derivative Works** | New code derived from DIMOS | Modified versions, forks, extended implementations |
| **Incorporated Software** | Products or services that use or incorporate DIMOS | Applications embedding DIMOS, research tools built on DIMOS |
| **Pull Requests** | Contributions submitted to NEC repository | Code contributions via GitHub pull requests |

A derivative work is created when:
- You modify any file in the `dimos/` package hierarchy
- You create new modules that inherit from or extend DIMOS classes
- You build software products that incorporate DIMOS functionality
- You develop services that use DIMOS as a component

**Sources:** [LICENSE:72-76](), [dimos/__init__.py:72-76]()

---

## Ownership and Licensing Model

### Intellectual Property Rights

The license establishes a dual-ownership model:

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Original Software"
        NEC_SOFT["DIMOS Core Software"]
        NEC_IP["NEC Intellectual Property Rights"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Derivative Works"
        LICENSEE_DW["Modified/Extended Code"]
        LICENSEE_IP["Licensee Intellectual Property Rights"]
    end
    
    subgraph "License Grants"
        TO_LICENSEE["License to Licensee:<br/>- Use original software<br/>- Create derivative works<br/>- Academic Use only"]
        TO_NEC["License to NEC:<br/>- Perpetual, irrevocable<br/>- Non-exclusive, royalty-free<br/>- Transferrable, sublicensable<br/>- Any purpose"]
    end
    
    NEC_IP --> NEC_SOFT
    NEC_SOFT --> TO_LICENSEE
    TO_LICENSEE --> LICENSEE_DW
    LICENSEE_IP --> LICENSEE_DW
    LICENSEE_DW --> TO_NEC
    
    style NEC_IP fill:#f9f9f9
    style LICENSEE_IP fill:#f9f9f9
```

**Key Ownership Principles:**

| Aspect | Original Software | Derivative Works |
|--------|------------------|------------------|
| **IP Rights Owner** | NEC Laboratories Europe GmbH | Licensee (your organization) |
| **License Grant** | Limited license to Licensee | Perpetual license to NEC |
| **Usage Rights** | Academic Use only | NEC: any purpose<br/>Licensee: Academic Use only |
| **Transferability** | Non-transferrable | NEC can transfer/sublicense |

**Sources:** [LICENSE:77-83](), [dimos/__init__.py:77-83]()

### Academic Use Restriction

Both the original software and all derivative works are restricted to Academic Use:

- **Permitted:** Use by accredited educational or research institutions for non-commercial purposes (academic research, teaching)
- **Prohibited:** Commercial use, distribution, resale, academic-commercial collaborations, commercial entity non-commercial use

For commercial use of derivative works, a separate commercial license agreement with NEC is required.

**Sources:** [LICENSE:96-99](), [LICENSE:307-309](), [dimos/__init__.py:96-99]()

---

## Source Code Provision Requirements

### Mandatory Repository Submission

All derivative works **must** be provided to NEC via the official repository:

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "Derivative Work Development"
        LOCAL["Local Development<br/>Repository"]
        DW_CODE["Derivative Work<br/>Source Code"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Submission Process"
        GITHUB["GitHub Repository<br/>https://github.com/nec-research/DIMOS"]
        METHODS["Submission Methods"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Submission Options"
        PR["Pull Request"]
        FORK["Forked Repository"]
        ISSUE["Issue with Archive"]
    end
    
    LOCAL --> DW_CODE
    DW_CODE --> METHODS
    METHODS --> PR
    METHODS --> FORK
    METHODS --> ISSUE
    PR --> GITHUB
    FORK --> GITHUB
    ISSUE --> GITHUB
```

**Repository Location:** `https://github.com/nec-research/DIMOS`

**Submission Methods:**

1. **Pull Request (Preferred):** Submit changes via GitHub pull request to the main repository
2. **Forked Repository:** Maintain a public fork linked to the original repository
3. **Issue Attachment:** Create an issue with source code archive attached

**Required Content:**

- Complete source code of all modifications
- All new files and modules created
- Modified versions of existing files (full file, not just diffs)
- Build scripts, configuration files if modified
- Test files for new functionality

**Sources:** [LICENSE:84-85](), [dimos/__init__.py:84-85]()

### Source Code Format Requirements

When providing source code:

| Requirement | Details |
|-------------|---------|
| **File Format** | Source files in original format (.py for Python) |
| **Structure** | Preserve directory structure relative to `dimos/` |
| **Completeness** | Include all dependencies not part of standard DIMOS |
| **Documentation** | Include inline comments explaining modifications |
| **Build Instructions** | Document any changes to build/installation process |

---

## Attribution Requirements

### Mandatory Notices

Three specific attribution requirements must be satisfied:

```mermaid
graph TD
    DW["Derivative Work"]
    
    subgraph "Required Notices"
        LICENSE_FILE["LICENSE File Copy"]
        BUILT_NOTICE["Built using NEC technology"]
        COPYRIGHT_NOTICE["Copyright Notice"]
    end
    
    subgraph "License File"
        FULL_TERMS["Complete NEC Software Library<br/>Academic Use Licence Terms"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Display Locations"
        DESC["Software Description"]
        WEBSITE["Website"]
        UI["User Interface"]
        ABOUT["About Page"]
        SPEC["Software Specification"]
        TECHDOC["Technical Documentation"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Notice Text File"
        NOTICE_TXT["NOTICE or similar file"]
        COPYRIGHT_TEXT["[Derivative Work] is licensed under<br/>the NEC Software Library Academic License.<br/>Copyright © 2025 NEC Laboratories Europe GmbH.<br/>All Rights Reserved."]
    end
    
    DW --> LICENSE_FILE
    DW --> BUILT_NOTICE
    DW --> COPYRIGHT_NOTICE
    
    LICENSE_FILE --> FULL_TERMS
    
    BUILT_NOTICE --> DESC
    BUILT_NOTICE --> WEBSITE
    BUILT_NOTICE --> UI
    BUILT_NOTICE --> ABOUT
    BUILT_NOTICE --> SPEC
    BUILT_NOTICE --> TECHDOC
    
    COPYRIGHT_NOTICE --> NOTICE_TXT
    NOTICE_TXT --> COPYRIGHT_TEXT
```

**Sources:** [LICENSE:86-94](), [dimos/__init__.py:86-94]()

### 1. License Terms Copy

**Requirement:** Include a complete copy of the license terms with the derivative work.

**Implementation:**
- Copy [LICENSE:1-372]() file to your derivative work's root directory
- Name it `LICENSE` or `LICENSE.txt`
- Do not modify the content
- Ensure it's included in all distributions

**Example Directory Structure:**
```
my-derivative-work/
├── LICENSE           # Copy of NEC Software Library Academic Use Licence Terms
├── README.md
├── setup.py
└── my_dimos_extension/
    └── __init__.py
```

### 2. "Built using NEC technology" Notice

**Requirement:** Prominently display the text "Built using NEC technology" in multiple locations.

**Display Locations:**

| Location | Implementation Example |
|----------|----------------------|
| **Software Description** | Include in package description in `setup.py` or `pyproject.toml` |
| **Website** | Add to homepage, footer, or about section |
| **User Interface** | Display in application about dialog or help screen |
| **About Page** | Create dedicated section for acknowledgments |
| **Software Specification** | Include in technical specifications document |
| **Technical Documentation** | Add to README.md and API documentation |

**Example Implementation (README.md):**
```markdown
# My Derivative Work

A molecular dynamics extension built on DIMOS.

**Built using NEC technology**

This software is built using the DIMOS framework developed by 
NEC Laboratories Europe GmbH.
```

**Example Implementation (Python About Function):**
```python
def display_about():
    print("My Derivative Work v1.0")
    print("Built using NEC technology")
    print("Based on DIMOS framework")
```

### 3. Copyright Notice in NOTICE File

**Requirement:** Include a specific copyright notice in a notice text file.

**Notice Text Template:**
```
[Derivative Work Name] is licensed under the NEC Software Library Academic 
License. Copyright © 2025 NEC Laboratories Europe GmbH. All Rights Reserved.
```

**Implementation:**
- Create a file named `NOTICE`, `NOTICE.txt`, or similar
- Include the complete notice text
- Replace `[Derivative Work Name]` with your actual project name
- Distribute this file with all copies of the derivative work

**Example NOTICE File:**
```
MyDIMOS Extension is licensed under the NEC Software Library Academic License. 
Copyright © 2025 NEC Laboratories Europe GmbH. All Rights Reserved.

This software is a derivative work based on DIMOS (Differentiable Molecular 
Simulator), developed by NEC Laboratories Europe GmbH.

For the complete license terms, see the LICENSE file.
```

**Sources:** [LICENSE:91-94](), [dimos/__init__.py:91-94]()

---

## Documentation Requirements

### Required Documentation Files

Create and maintain the following documentation:

| File | Purpose | Required Content |
|------|---------|-----------------|
| **README.md** | Project overview | Purpose, installation, usage, NEC attribution |
| **LICENSE** | License terms | Complete copy of NEC license |
| **NOTICE** | Copyright notice | Required copyright statement |
| **CHANGELOG.md** | Modification history | List of changes from original DIMOS |
| **CONTRIBUTING.md** | Contribution guide | How others can contribute to derivative work |

### Code Documentation

**In-File Headers:**

Every modified or new file should include:

```python
# This file is part of [Derivative Work Name], a derivative work of DIMOS
# DIMOS Copyright © 2025 NEC Laboratories Europe GmbH
# 
# [Derivative Work Name] modifications Copyright © [Year] [Your Organization]
# Licensed under the NEC Software Library Academic Use License
#
# Original DIMOS source: [path to original file if applicable]
# Modifications: [brief description of changes]

# [Rest of file content...]
```

**Modification Comments:**

Mark significant changes in code:

```python
def calculate_energy(self, positions):
    # Original DIMOS implementation
    energy = self._compute_bonded(positions)
    
    # MODIFICATION: Added custom correction term for [specific purpose]
    # Author: [Your Name], [Date]
    energy += self._custom_correction(positions)
    
    return energy
```

**Sources:** [LICENSE:86-87](), [dimos/__init__.py:86-87]()

## Practical Development Workflow

### Development Process

```mermaid
graph TB
    START["Start Development"]
    FORK["Fork DIMOS Repository<br/>(if using GitHub workflow)"]
    CLONE["Clone to Local Environment"]
    
    subgraph "Development Cycle"
        MODIFY["Modify DIMOS Code"]
        TEST["Run Tests"]
        DOCUMENT["Document Changes"]
        COMMIT["Commit to Local Repository"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Compliance Check"
        CHECK_LICENSE["Verify LICENSE file included"]
        CHECK_NOTICE["Verify NOTICE file correct"]
        CHECK_ATTR["Verify 'Built using NEC' displayed"]
        CHECK_HEADERS["Verify file headers updated"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Submission"
        PREPARE["Prepare Source Archive"]
        SUBMIT_PR["Submit Pull Request<br/>OR"]
        SUBMIT_ISSUE["Create Issue with Archive<br/>OR"]
        MAINTAIN_FORK["Maintain Public Fork"]
    end
    
    START --> FORK
    FORK --> CLONE
    CLONE --> MODIFY
    MODIFY --> TEST
    TEST --> DOCUMENT
    DOCUMENT --> COMMIT
    COMMIT --> MODIFY
    
    COMMIT --> CHECK_LICENSE
    CHECK_LICENSE --> CHECK_NOTICE
    CHECK_NOTICE --> CHECK_ATTR
    CHECK_ATTR --> CHECK_HEADERS
    
    CHECK_HEADERS --> PREPARE
    PREPARE --> SUBMIT_PR
    PREPARE --> SUBMIT_ISSUE
    PREPARE --> MAINTAIN_FORK
    
    SUBMIT_PR --> END["Derivative Work Complete"]
    SUBMIT_ISSUE --> END
    MAINTAIN_FORK --> END
```

**Sources:** [LICENSE:72-99](), [dimos/__init__.py:72-99]()

### File Organization Best Practices

Organize your derivative work to clearly distinguish original and modified code:

```
my-dimos-derivative/
├── LICENSE                          # Required: NEC license copy
├── NOTICE                           # Required: Copyright notice
├── README.md                        # Required: Include attribution
├── setup.py                         # Include attribution in description
├── dimos/                          # Original DIMOS code (if including)
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── energy.py
│   └── ...
├── dimos_extensions/               # Your new modules
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── custom_integrator.py       # New integration methods
│   └── enhanced_constraints.py    # New constraint algorithms
├── modified/                       # Modified DIMOS files (clearly separated)
│   ├── README.md                  # Explain what was modified and why
│   ├── energy_modified.py         # Modified version of dimos/energy.py
│   └── constraints_modified.py    # Modified version of dimos/constraints.py
├── tests/                          # Tests for modifications
│   ├── test_custom_integrator.py
│   └── test_enhanced_constraints.py
└── docs/                           # Documentation
    ├── modifications.md           # Detailed change log
    └── api.md                     # API documentation
```

### Compliance Checklist

Before submission, verify:

- [ ] **Source Code Provision**
  - [ ] All modified files included
  - [ ] All new files included
  - [ ] Directory structure preserved
  - [ ] Submission method chosen (PR/fork/issue)

- [ ] **License Files**
  - [ ] LICENSE file copied from original DIMOS
  - [ ] LICENSE file unmodified
  - [ ] LICENSE file in root directory

- [ ] **Attribution**
  - [ ] NOTICE file created with required text
  - [ ] "Built using NEC technology" in README.md
  - [ ] "Built using NEC technology" in software description
  - [ ] "Built using NEC technology" in UI/about page (if applicable)
  - [ ] "Built using NEC technology" in technical documentation

- [ ] **File Headers**
  - [ ] Copyright headers in all modified files
  - [ ] Copyright headers in all new files
  - [ ] Original file references included (for modified files)

- [ ] **Documentation**
  - [ ] README.md explains modifications
  - [ ] CHANGELOG.md documents changes
  - [ ] Inline code comments explain modifications
  - [ ] Modification markers in code

- [ ] **Repository Submission**
  - [ ] GitHub repository URL: `https://github.com/nec-research/DIMOS`
  - [ ] Pull request created OR
  - [ ] Public fork maintained OR
  - [ ] Issue with archive created

**Sources:** [LICENSE:84-94](), [dimos/__init__.py:84-94]()

## Common Scenarios

### Scenario 1: Bug Fix

**Situation:** You discover and fix a bug in [dimos/energy.py]().

**Requirements:**
1. Submit fixed version via pull request
2. Include license terms with submission
3. Add modification comment in code
4. If distributing separately, include all attribution

**Example Modification:**
```python
# File: dimos/energy.py
# MODIFICATION: Fixed numerical stability issue in Ewald summation
# Author: [Your Name], [Date]
# Original issue: Division by zero when cutoff equals box size

def compute_ewald_correction(self, positions, cutoff, box_size):
    # Original code had potential division by zero
    # if cutoff == box_size / 2:
    #     factor = 1.0 / (cutoff - box_size / 2)  # Division by zero!
    
    # FIXED: Added safety check
    denominator = cutoff - box_size / 2
    if abs(denominator) < 1e-10:
        denominator = 1e-10
    factor = 1.0 / denominator
    
    return factor * self._correction_term(positions)
```

### Scenario 2: New Feature Module

**Situation:** You develop a new integrator class that extends DIMOS functionality.

**Requirements:**
1. Create new module file with proper header
2. If distributing as package, include LICENSE, NOTICE, README.md
3. Display "Built using NEC technology" in package description
4. Submit source code to NEC repository

**Example New File:**
```python
# custom_integrator.py
# Part of MyDIMOS Extension
# Copyright © 2025 [Your Organization]
#
# Built using NEC technology
# This is a derivative work of DIMOS, developed by NEC Laboratories Europe GmbH
# Licensed under the NEC Software Library Academic Use License

from dimos.integrators import Integrator
import torch

class AdaptiveTimestepIntegrator(Integrator):
    """
    Custom integrator with adaptive timestep control.
    
    This is a derivative work extending the DIMOS Integrator class
    with automatic timestep adjustment based on energy conservation.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, initial_timestep=0.001, tolerance=1e-5):
        super().__init__()
        self.timestep = initial_timestep
        self.tolerance = tolerance
    
    # ... implementation ...
```

### Scenario 3: Modified Simulation Loop

**Situation:** You modify [dimos/simulation.py]() to add custom logging.

**Requirements:**
1. Provide complete modified simulation.py file
2. Document all changes in file and CHANGELOG
3. Include modification markers in code
4. Submit via GitHub

**Example Project Structure:**
```
enhanced-dimos-logging/
├── LICENSE                    # Copy of NEC license
├── NOTICE                     # Required copyright notice
├── README.md                  # Includes "Built using NEC technology"
├── CHANGELOG.md              # Documents simulation.py changes
├── modified/
│   └── simulation.py         # Modified version with change markers
└── examples/
    └── demo_enhanced_logging.py
```

**Sources:** [LICENSE:72-99](), [dimos/__init__.py:72-99]()

---

## Legal Considerations

### Commercial Use Prohibition

**Important:** Derivative works are subject to the same Academic Use restriction as the original software.

**Prohibited Activities:**
- Commercial distribution of derivative works
- Use in commercial products or services
- Academic-commercial collaborations using derivative works
- Any commercial entity use (even non-commercial purposes)

**Remedy:** For commercial use, contact NEC to negotiate a commercial license agreement.

**Sources:** [LICENSE:96-99](), [LICENSE:307-309](), [dimos/__init__.py:96-99]()

### Indemnification

The licensee is responsible for:
- Ensuring compliance with all terms
- Indemnifying NEC against third-party claims related to derivative works
- Proper use of derivative works by representatives (employees, students, contractors)

**Sources:** [LICENSE:192-197](), [dimos/__init__.py:192-197]()

### License Termination

The license can be terminated if:
- Requirements for derivative works are not met
- Source code is not provided to NEC
- Attribution requirements are not satisfied
- Commercial use occurs without separate agreement

Upon termination, all use must cease and copies must be destroyed.

**Sources:** [LICENSE:223-246](), [dimos/__init__.py:223-246]()

## Summary

### Essential Requirements Table

| Requirement | Mandatory | Location |
|-------------|-----------|----------|
| Provide source code to NEC | ✓ Yes | https://github.com/nec-research/DIMOS |
| Include LICENSE file copy | ✓ Yes | Root directory of derivative work |
| Include NOTICE file | ✓ Yes | Root directory with specific text |
| Display "Built using NEC technology" | ✓ Yes | Multiple visible locations |
| Grant license to NEC | ✓ Yes | Automatic upon creation |
| Academic Use only | ✓ Yes | All uses of derivative work |
| Maintain file headers | ✓ Recommended | All modified and new files |
| Document changes | ✓ Recommended | CHANGELOG.md and inline comments |
